html:
Wall paintings that cover the three rooms of a small temple at Bonampak, a Maya site in Chiapas, Mexico, painted around 790 CE. They are the best preserved Maya murals known.

The rooms tell one story in sequence:

  • Room 1: the court, with lords in white mantles, musicians and masked dancers, as a royal heir is presented.
  • Room 2: a fierce battle and, after it, captives stripped and bleeding before the king Yajaw Chan Muwaan.
  • Room 3: a victory celebration with dancers in great feathered costumes and nobles drawing blood in ritual.

Bonampak was a small dependency of nearby Yaxchilan, and the murals were made just before the Classic Maya cities fell into decline. Their vivid scenes of war and sacrifice changed how scholars saw the Maya, who had once been imagined as peaceful star watchers. Lacandon Maya guided outsiders to the site in 1946.
